lesson.title: The Closest Point Problem: Squaring the Distance to Simplify the Search
lesson.summary: Find the point on a parabola closest to a given external point by minimizing squared distance instead of distance itself, avoiding a messy square root derivative.
lesson.body:
Minimizing distance almost always benefits from a small trick: instead of minimizing the distance function D(x) directly, minimize D(x)^2. Because squaring is an increasing function for nonnegative numbers, whatever x minimizes D(x)^2 also minimizes D(x), and D(x)^2 has no square root in it, which makes the derivative far cleaner. This trick is the entire reason the closest point problem is approachable by hand.

Consider the parabola y = x^2 and the external point P = (3, 0). A general point on the parabola can be written (x, x^2), so the squared distance from that point to P is f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + (x^2 - 0)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + x^4. Expanding gives f(x) = x^4 + x^2 - 6x + 9.

Differentiate: f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2x - 6. Setting this equal to zero gives 4x^3 + 2x - 6 = 0, or after dividing by 2, 2x^3 + x - 3 = 0. Testing x = 1 gives 2(1) + 1 - 3 = 0, so x = 1 is a root. Factoring out (x - 1) gives 2x^3 + x - 3 = (x - 1)(2x^2 + 2x + 3). The remaining quadratic factor 2x^2 + 2x + 3 has discriminant 2^2 - 4(2)(3) = 4 - 24 = -20, which is negative, so it contributes no real roots. That means x = 1 is the only real critical point, and there is no other candidate to compare it against.

Verify with the second derivative: f''(x) = 12x^2 + 2, which is positive for every real x, since 12x^2 is never negative and 2 is added on top. Because f''(x) is positive everywhere, f is concave up across its whole domain, confirming that x = 1 is not just a local minimum but the global minimum of squared distance.

The closest point on the parabola is therefore (1, 1^2) = (1, 1), and the minimum distance is the square root of f(1): f(1) = (1-3)^2 + 1^2 = 4 + 1 = 5, so the distance is sqrt(5), approximately 2.236 units.

Notice something the earlier fencing and box problems did not have: there was no domain restriction to check here at all. The parabola y = x^2 is defined for every real x, with no physical wall cutting off part of it, so the practical domain is all real numbers and there is no endpoint to compare against. That is worth flagging explicitly, because not every optimization problem has boundaries to worry about, and recognizing when a domain is unbounded in both directions (paired here with a second derivative that never changes sign) is itself part of verifying that a critical point is the true global answer.
